item.title: Two-step optimism, three-step totality: paired witnesses for reliable broadcast
item.description: Reliable broadcast lets one designated party, the broadcaster, hand a value to nnn parties so that the honest ones end up agreeing on it, even when up to fff of them are Byzantine, meaning they can behave arbitrarily. DAG-based consensus protocols run one broadcast instance per block per round. Every step a broadcast takes therefore shows up in commit latency, and every step by which one honest party can lag behind another shows up in how long timeouts must be.

item.title: Narwhal and Tusk: Moving the Bottleneck Out of BFT Consensus
item.description: For most of the last decade, work on fast Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus has focused on one number: message complexity, meaning how many protocol messages the validators exchange per decision. HotStuff (Yin et al., 2019) brought that number down to linear in the partially synchronous setting by routing all votes through a leader. The paper by Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino and Spiegelman, published at EuroSys 2022, argues that this target misses where the cost actually sits in a real ledger. The expensive part is not agreeing on an order. It is moving the transactions themselves to every validator, reliably.

item.title: A BFT ordering service for Fabric, and the library under it
item.description: Fabric’s ordering service receives endorsed transactions from clients and emits a stream of blocks. When we wrote this paper the latest release, v2.3, ran it on Raft, which tolerates crashes and nothing worse. The paper describes how my co-authors and I made Fabric Byzantine fault-tolerant end to end: a consensus library in Go, based on the BFT-SMaRt protocol, and the changes to the orderer, the peer and the client that had to come with it.

item.title: About
item.description:
I’m Artem Barger. I lead R&D at Modelyo, where I work on confidential computing: trusted execution environments, attestation, and what it takes to deploy them for real.

Before that I spent most of a decade on permissioned blockchains. At IBM Research in Haifa I was one of the authors of Hyperledger Fabric and later managed the blockchain group. I worked on Fabric’s gossip layer, service discovery and its Byzantine fault-tolerant ordering service, and I served on the Hyperledger Technical Steering Committee.

item.title: Why this blog
item.description:
Most of what I know about distributed systems I learned from papers, and most of the papers I meant to read I never got to. The list only grows. The name of this blog is an admission of that: everything on the list gets read, eventually.

This is where the reading happens in public. Each post takes one paper and tries to answer what I would ask a colleague who had read it. What problem is it solving? Why did the existing answers fall short? What is the actual idea, and what does it cost? If a theorem carries the result, I explain what it says and what it assumes. If a diagram makes the design clearer than three paragraphs would, there is a diagram.
